concept: Agentic UX oversight, approval and recovery
summary: Source-anchored research for Agentic UX oversight, approval and recovery. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: AWS recommends approval timeouts, escalation, and a safe fallback, typically blocking the operation, when nobody responds within the defined window. The interface should not leave an unanswered approval waiting indefinitely. (low confidence)

AWS recommends retaining who reviewed an approval, when notification and response occurred, which operation was reviewed, the decision, and any escalation events, so the approval history can be reconstructed. (low confidence)

Escalation should be a designed recovery path: offer clarification, alternatives or expert intervention for ambiguity, and preserve a resumable plan for human takeover when the agent gets stuck. (medium confidence)

Data & Society argues that a pause button alone does not establish meaningful oversight: the user must be able to notice a problem, observe the relevant work and redirect it. Its research agenda also warns that a complete tool-call trace may still fail to explain a strategy change. (low confidence)

Recovery messages should identify completed work, the failed step, and a concrete continuation path. Institute of AI PM recommends distinguishing succeeded, failed, and unattempted steps; Ditto illustrates an upload failure message that explains what succeeded, why the next item failed, whether anything was sent, and how to continue. (medium confidence)

For recovery, provide an action history and an available reversal path; when reversal expires, communicate that limit. Smashing Magazine recommends chronological action logs and explicit undo windows; HatchWorks recommends receipts describing changes and rollback options. (medium confidence)

Before execution, show a readable plan and give users ways to approve it, edit it, or take control. Institute of AI PM also recommends cancellation before execution rather than forcing approval of the whole plan. (medium confidence)

Use risk-tiered approvals rather than sending every action to review. AWS warns that indiscriminate review creates fatigue and rubber-stamp approvals; Smashing Magazine describes different autonomy levels for low-stakes and high-stakes tasks. (medium confidence)

When a decision needs human judgment, provide an escalation path instead of silently continuing. Smashing Magazine proposes clarification, choices, and human-expert intervention; AWS calls for escalation when a primary reviewer is unavailable. (medium confidence)

A VS Code issue author reported that an agent created many checkpoints visible in a Git extension and that an attempt to disable checkpoint creation did not help. This is an attributed usability complaint, not proof of present behavior or a released fix. (low confidence)

Make the scope of delegated authority explicit and adjustable: Smashing Magazine recommends autonomy settings per task type, while AWS recommends narrowly scoped, auditable and revocable persistent trust grants rather than wildcard grants. (medium confidence)

Smashing Magazine recommends setting agent autonomy per task type, allowing confirmation for one task and pre-approved autonomous action for another. Its example separates scheduling from sending email. (low confidence)

Approval interfaces should make the proposed action and consequences understandable before consent. AWS calls for relevant data sources and decision context in the approval interface; Institute of AI PM calls for disclosure of affected resources and people. (medium confidence)

Show action state in a readable timeline. Institute of AI PM recommends completed, current, and remaining steps; Smashing Magazine recommends indicating whether an action succeeded, is in progress, or was undone. (medium confidence)

Institute of AI PM recommends a clear way to check status and pause background work, and real-time visibility that lets users interrupt before consequential tool use. These are practitioner recommendations, not demonstrated cancellation guarantees. (low confidence)

A Hermes feature-request author reported being unable to recover deleted or overwritten files and proposed Git-backed snapshots before destructive operations and a rollback command. This establishes a reported recovery need and a proposed remedy, not the current availability of that remedy. (low confidence)

Visible progress should distinguish work in progress, successful actions and undone actions; practitioner guidance also recommends a current-step indicator and links to produced artifacts in an activity timeline. (medium confidence)

HatchWorks recommends explicit start, stop, pause and resume controls for asynchronous agents, with defined stop behavior for in-flight tool calls, queued actions, partial completion and rollback messaging. This is design guidance, not evidence that cancelling a task reverses actions already completed. (low confidence)
